Harmonic Mean Sangaku

GeometryTrianglesFractions
Game: Two ladders lean between two walls; watch where they cross as you move the walls.
How to play: Drag A, B, D or E with a mouse or finger, or focus a point and use the arrow keys. Press Check the identity to test what you see.
Look for the math

Two ladders cross between upright walls. The surprising part is that the height of the crossing does not change when you slide the walls apart or together; it is decided only by the two wall heights. This page claims an exact recipe for that height, and the logic test checks it on thousands of pictures.

A height that stays put

Call the wall heights AE and BD, and the distance between the feet AB. Let the ladders meet at P, and call the point of the ground below P by the name C, so its height is CP. Moving the feet changes AB and moves C along the ground, but CP stays the same. The logic test compares CP at wall distances 5 and 500 for every pair of wall heights from 1 to 40 and finds the same number each time.

Two pairs of matching triangles

Write AC = x and BC = y. Because the walls are upright, triangle ABD and the smaller triangle ACP are similar triangles, so their sides are in the same ratio:

(x + y) / x = BD / CP = 1 + y / x, hence y / x = (BD − CP) / CP.

The ladders BE and the small triangle CBP give the other pair: x / y = (AE − CP) / CP. Both proportions are checked for every even pair of wall heights up to 30 in the logic test.

Multiply, then take reciprocals

Multiplying the two proportions cancels x / y and leaves (AE − CP)(BD − CP) = CP². Expanding and simplifying gives AE·BD = CP·(AE + BD). Divide through by AE·BD·CP and the page's claim appears:

1 / CP = 1 / AE + 1 / BD

Since the harmonic mean of AE and BD is 2·AE·BD / (AE + BD), this says CP = H(AE, BD) / 2. The test verifies both forms for 6,400 positive configurations, and also for walls of negative (directed) height.

How this differs from Harmonic Mean

The applet HarmonicMean is a bug race about average speed; its page lists many places the harmonic mean turns up, including the 1877 sangaku, where it states CP = ½·H(a, b). HarmonicMeanSangaku is the dedicated diagram for that sangaku: you drag the four points A, B, D and E, and the applet can show the point names and horizontal guide lines. Its page writes the same fact as a reciprocal identity and stresses that the crossing height does not depend on the wall spacing. The two statements agree; neither contradicts the other. The original skips the calculation when the wall feet are less than one unit apart and gets no crossing when the ladders are parallel — the port keeps both behaviours.

Try making one wall much taller than the other, then slide the feet far apart: the crossing stays at the same height above the ground.
